questions.q: What is the security problem in the action below?
questions.hint: Who has ROLE_USER? And what comes back when you change {id}?

options.text: Any logged-in user can change the id and download someone else's file, because there is no ownership check
options.why: `ROLE_USER` only says the person is logged in. To check whether the document is theirs you would need a voter or a query that filters by owner.

options.text: Using `ROLE_ADMIN` instead of `ROLE_USER` would fix it
options.why: Then ordinary users couldn't even download their own files. The problem is not at the role level but in object ownership.

options.text: Using POST instead of GET would make it safe
options.why: Changing the HTTP method does not add an ownership check; changing the id in a POST is just as easy.

options.text: There is no problem, since `#[IsGranted]` is already there
options.why: `#[IsGranted]` is there, but it only checks the role. It has no idea which document is being requested.

questions.q: Sarah's session has expired and she calls `/api/orders`. Josh, while logged in, tries to delete someone else's order. Who gets which status code?
questions.hint: Whose identity does the server not know, and whose identity does it know but lack permission?

options.text: Sarah gets 403, Josh gets 401
options.why: That is backwards. 401 is for missing identity, 403 for missing permission.

options.text: Sarah gets 401, Josh gets 403
options.why: Sarah's proof of identity is no longer valid, so she must log in (401). The server knows Josh, but he has no permission for the action (403).

options.text: Both get 401
options.why: If Josh got a 401, his app would make him log in again, yet logging in would change nothing because the permission itself is missing.

options.text: Both get 400 Bad Request
options.why: 400 means the request is malformed. Here the requests are fine; the issue is identity and permission.

questions.q: Which of these are authorization tasks (not authentication)?
questions.hint: Which ones answer "what can you do" rather than "who are you"?

options.text: Checking a password
options.why: Matching a password verifies proof of identity. That is authentication.

options.text: Checking whether an order belongs to this user
options.why: Deciding whether a user may act on one specific thing is object-level authorization.

options.text: Letting only ROLE_ADMIN into the `/api/admin` path
options.why: The identity is already known; what is being decided is whether this user may enter this area. That is authorization.

options.text: Verifying a token's signature
options.why: Signature verification tells you whether the token is genuine, that is, whether the proof of identity is valid. That is authentication.

options.text: Deciding whether the user may delete an invoice
options.why: Whether an action is allowed, yes or no, is exactly what an authorization decision is.

questions.q: In Symfony, which part works out the user's identity from the request?
questions.hint: At the courier office, who looks at the ID: the counter, or the parcel register?

options.text: A voter
options.why: A voter doesn't find the identity; it takes an already-known identity and decides on permission.

options.text: `access_control`
options.why: `access_control` matches URL and role to let someone in or block them. That is an authorization layer.

options.text: The firewall's authenticator
options.why: The authenticator reads the cookie, password or token and finds the user. That is authentication.

options.text: `#[IsGranted]`
options.why: `#[IsGranted]` is a permission guard on an action; the identity has already been settled before it runs.

questions.q: The `/api/invoices` list holds 10,000 invoices from many companies. What is the best way to keep other companies' invoices out of the response?
questions.hint: Do other people's rows need to leave the database at all?

options.text: Fetch every invoice and run a voter on each one in a loop
options.why: It works, but it is slow, breaks pagination counts, and pulls other people's data into memory for no reason.

options.text: Filter by the logged-in user's company in the query itself
options.why: Other companies' rows never leave the database. It is fast, pagination stays correct, and there is less room for mistakes.

options.text: Send everything and filter in Vue, showing only the user's own
options.why: By then the data has already reached the browser; anyone can open the Network tab and see it all.

options.text: Ask the client to send `?companyId=`
options.why: The client could then send any companyId, which is exactly the IDOR problem.

questions.q: The team put `INVOICE_VIEW` on GET. Which route is still open to a logged-in stranger?
questions.hint: Same URL, different method. Which one checks whose invoice it is?

options.text: DELETE: it only checks that the user is logged in
options.why: ROLE_USER says nothing about ownership. Give it its own voter attribute and test it.

options.text: GET: voters don't work on read actions
options.why: The voter on GET is exactly what protects the read.

options.text: Neither: the voter on GET also covers DELETE
options.why: Attributes belong to one action each. A guard on one method protects only that method.

questions.q: A team did the following to stop IDOR. Which ones actually protect?
questions.hint: Which ones check on the server, and which just make things harder or hide them?

options.text: Checking ownership with a voter on every object
options.why: This is the core fix: whatever the id is, if the thing isn't the user's, the answer is 403.

options.text: Replacing auto-increment ids with UUIDs
options.why: Guessing gets harder, but once an id leaks the data is open. It is an extra hurdle, not a fix.

options.text: Taking identity from `#[CurrentUser]`, not from a `userId` in the body
options.why: The identity then comes from the verified session or token; the client can't claim to be someone else.

options.text: Hiding links and buttons to other people's data in Vue
options.why: Hiding things in the UI doesn't close the endpoint; when the API is called directly, the server is the only guard.

questions.q: A company wants a banned user's access cut off immediately. Which design gives that most easily?
questions.hint: Does the server look anything up on each request?

options.text: A self-contained JWT valid for 30 days
options.why: The server only checks signature and expiry, so the token would keep working for 30 days even after the ban.

options.text: A server-side session, or an opaque token checked against the database
options.why: The store is consulted on every request; delete the row and the token is dead.

options.text: Writing `banned: false` in the JWT payload
options.why: The payload of a token that has already been issued can't be changed.

options.text: Asking the user to log out themselves
options.why: A ban is the server's decision; you can't depend on the user's cooperation.

questions.q: This JWT has the payload `{"sub":"42","email":"a@x.com","password":"1234","exp":1893456000}`. What is wrong?
questions.hint: Who can read a JWT payload?

options.text: Nothing, a JWT is signed
options.why: A signature prevents tampering; it provides no confidentiality.

options.text: The payload is only base64-encoded, so anyone can read the password
options.why: Whoever gets the token can decode the payload and see the password. Nothing confidential belongs in a payload.

options.text: It should contain only the `exp` field and nothing else
options.why: Harmless fields like sub and exp are fine; the problem is only the confidential data.

questions.q: Which of these are benefits of the access + refresh token design?
questions.hint: Which ones shrink the window of damage and make revocation possible?

options.text: If an access token is stolen, the damage window is limited to 15 minutes
options.why: Because the lifetime is short, a thief doesn't hold a working token for long.

options.text: The refresh token lives in the database, so logout or a ban can revoke it
options.why: Delete the row and no new access token can be obtained.

options.text: The server never has to remember any state again
options.why: Revocation is possible precisely because the refresh token is remembered; the design is not fully stateless.

options.text: Token theft becomes impossible
options.why: Theft isn't prevented; only the damage is limited.

questions.q: Ryan's admin deletes Sarah's refresh tokens at 10:00. Her 15-minute access token was issued at 09:55. When is she locked out?
questions.hint: What does the API check on each request, and when does the token stop passing it?

options.text: At 10:00, the moment the tokens are deleted
options.why: The API only checks the access token's signature and expiry, so it never learns about the deletion.

options.text: At 10:10, when the access token expires and no refresh is possible
options.why: The token passes until its own expiry. After that, the refresh needs a database row, and there is none.

options.text: After 29 days, when the refresh token expires
options.why: The refresh row was deleted, so it can't be used at all. Only the short access token is left to run out.

options.text: Never, because she still holds an access token
options.why: An access token dies on its expiry date, and without a refresh token she can't get another.

questions.q: Which piece of code puts a developer's users at the most risk?
questions.code:
const res = await api.post('/api/login', creds)
localStorage.setItem('refreshToken', res.refreshToken)
questions.hint: If the page has an XSS hole, who can read this?

options.text: The refresh token is in localStorage, where an XSS script can read it and send it to its own server
options.why: Any script on the page can read everything in localStorage, so a long-lived token can be stolen.

options.text: It should use GET instead of POST
options.why: Using GET for login would put the password in the URL and logs, which is even worse.

options.text: Using async/await is the problem
options.why: That has nothing to do with security.

questions.q: Someone calls `/api/token/refresh` with a refresh token that was already spent. What should the server do?
questions.hint: What could it mean that one token shows up twice?

options.text: Quietly issue new tokens
options.why: Then a thief could keep refreshing indefinitely.

options.text: Reject only that one request with a 401 and do nothing else
options.why: You can't tell the real user from the thief; unless you cut off the whole token family, the thief can carry on through another branch.

options.text: Revoke all of that user's refresh tokens and require a fresh login
options.why: Reuse means the token family has leaked; revoking everything shuts the thief out, and the real user logs in again.

questions.q: Which of these reduce the damage from token theft?
questions.hint: Which ones keep JavaScript away from the token or shrink the window?

options.text: Keeping the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie
options.why: An XSS script can't read it.

options.text: Giving the access token a 15-minute lifetime
options.why: Even if stolen, it works for only a short time.

options.text: Keeping the token in localStorage because it's simpler than a cookie
options.why: It is simpler, but any XSS can read it.

options.text: Making the token last 1 year so users aren't annoyed
options.why: A long lifetime makes the damage window huge.

questions.q: An SPA developer is adding Google login. Which approach is right?
questions.hint: Can an SPA hide a secret?

options.text: Implicit flow: take the token directly from the URL fragment
options.why: The token leaks into browser history, logs and the referrer; this flow is now abandoned.

options.text: Code flow + PKCE, without a client secret
options.why: An SPA is a public client with nowhere to keep a secret. PKCE fills that gap.

options.text: Code flow with the client_secret kept in JavaScript
options.why: Anything in the browser is visible to everyone in DevTools; the secret is no longer secret.

options.text: Taking the user's Google password and logging in from the server
options.why: That is precisely the habit OAuth was created to end: handing a password to an app.

questions.q: Someone sends an OAuth2 access token to your app and wants to log in with it. What do you do?
questions.hint: Does an access token say who it was issued for?

options.text: Log them in if the signature checks out
options.why: The token might have been issued for another app; a token doesn't prove who someone is.

options.text: Just ask for their email
options.why: An email sent by the client isn't proof; an attacker can send any email.

options.text: Ask for an OIDC id_token and verify iss, aud, exp and nonce
options.why: The id_token is what says who the user is and whether the token was issued for this very login of ours.

questions.q: What mistake does the code below make?
questions.hint: Where is the proof that this returning request is one we started ourselves?

options.text: It has no state check, no id_token claim check, and it uses the email as the key
options.why: No state means CSRF, no claim checks means forged tokens, and the stable `sub` should be used instead of the email.

options.text: The route doesn't specify a method
options.why: That is minor; the real hole is the missing verification.

options.text: No mistake, since a code can only be used once
options.why: Even if a code is single-use, with CSRF the attacker's own code can slip in.

questions.q: Which of these are correct practice for OAuth2/OIDC?
questions.hint: Which ones avoid assuming instead of verifying?

options.text: Create a random state and nonce each time and keep them in the session
options.why: Matching them on return blocks CSRF and token replay.

options.text: Register the full redirect_uri exactly at the IdP
options.why: This closes the path for a code or token to reach an attacker's URL.

options.text: Identify users by email, not by `sub`
options.why: An email can change or be reused; the stable key is `sub`.

options.text: Keep the client_secret in a script and fetch the token from the browser
options.why: A secret in the browser is not secret.

questions.q: A large customer says, "We want to log in with our Okta, we use SAML." What does that mean?
questions.hint: Are SAML's job and OIDC's job different problems?

options.text: They want to give the app permission to read their files
options.why: Permission to files is OAuth2's job; what is being asked for here is corporate login (SSO).

options.text: Their employees will log in at the company's IdP, and the IdP will send our app a signed XML assertion saying who they are
options.why: SAML is the XML-based form of corporate SSO, the older counterpart of what OIDC does.

options.text: We have to keep their passwords in our database
options.why: The whole point of SSO is that passwords stay with the IdP and never reach us.

questions.q: Which statements about PKCE are correct?
questions.hint: Think about how the verifier and the challenge relate.

options.text: code_challenge is the SHA-256 hash of code_verifier
options.why: With the S256 method, challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), a one-way function.

options.text: The original code_verifier is sent when requesting the token
options.why: The server hashes it and compares it to the challenge from the start.

options.text: It is only for mobile apps and isn't needed on the web
options.why: It is mandatory for public clients and now recommended for server-side apps too.

options.text: With PKCE you no longer need state
options.why: state prevents CSRF and PKCE prevents code theft; they do different jobs.

questions.q: Every time a new department opens, Ryan has to create a new role like `ROLE_MANAGER_<DEPARTMENT>` and change code. What is the right fix?
questions.hint: Is a department a user's title, or a fact about the thing?

options.text: Keep making a separate role for each department
options.why: The number of roles multiplies, and every new department needs a deploy.

options.text: Keep a single `ROLE_MANAGER` and compare the department in the voter
options.why: Department is a fact about the thing and the user. Checking it in the voter means a new department needs no code change.

options.text: Give every manager `ROLE_ADMIN`
options.why: Allowing everyone everything means abolishing the rule.

options.text: Hide buttons by department in Vue
options.why: Hiding things in the UI leaves the API open; the check has to be on the server.

questions.q: What is the problem with the voter below?
questions.hint: What is returned for an unrecognized attribute? And has anyone checked who the user is?

options.text: An unrecognized attribute returns true, and the user and role are never checked at all
options.why: Anyone can approve an expense under $500, and every other attribute is allowed for everybody. The default should be false.

options.text: Only the `<=` is wrong; it should be `<`
options.why: Where the limit falls is a business decision; the real problem is security.

options.text: No problem, since the controller uses `#[IsGranted]`
options.why: `#[IsGranted]` just calls the voter. Whatever the voter says is the decision.

questions.q: The company adds a `/api/expenses/export.csv` route and nobody writes a rule for it. Which setup keeps it closed?
questions.hint: What should a voter say about an action nobody has thought about yet?

options.text: A voter that claims only known attributes and ends in `default => false`, plus `#[IsGranted]` on the new action
options.why: The unknown action is refused until a rule is written on purpose, and the guard makes the route's permission visible in review.

options.text: A voter whose last line is `return true`, so nothing ever breaks
options.why: Nothing breaks for the attacker either: every new action is open to everyone from day one.

options.text: Guarding only `GET /expenses/{id}`, since export is just a read
options.why: The export route is a separate action. An unguarded route lets any employee download every expense.

questions.q: In a project, a member can see every task, and only the lead can delete tasks. Which model is simplest?
questions.hint: What is the permission coming from, a relationship to what?

options.text: ABAC, based on the money amount
options.why: There is no amount or time here; the permission comes from the user's relationship to the project.

options.text: ReBAC: look at the user's relation (member, lead) to the project
options.why: Permission follows from whether a relationship exists and of what kind; a voter that looks up a grants table is enough.

options.text: A separate role for every project
options.why: More projects means more roles; relationship data belongs in the data.

questions.q: In which situations is a separate policy engine (OPA, Cedar, OpenFGA) justified?
questions.hint: Is a handful of rules in a single monolith a good enough reason?

options.text: We want to change the same rules across many services at once
options.why: With the rules in one place, you don't have to change code in every service.

options.text: The rules need to change regularly without a deploy
options.why: Rules kept outside the code can be changed and audited separately.

options.text: One Symfony app has three rules
options.why: Voters handle that; an extra service only adds complexity.

options.text: We don't enjoy writing `if` on the server
options.why: That is not a reason; voters are exactly what keeps those `if`s organized.

questions.q: Sarah is a manager, and she tries to approve a $300 expense that she submitted herself. What does ExpenseVoter return?
questions.hint: Reread the rules: which one is broken here?

options.text: true, because she is a manager and the amount is under the limit
options.why: The last condition (not their own expense) is broken; all the conditions must match together.

options.text: false, because the requester and the approver are the same person
options.why: Separation of duties: the `getRequester() !== $user` condition blocks it, so the response is 403.

options.text: false, because managers can never approve
options.why: Managers can; one specific condition is stopping this.

questions.q: What caution is needed about the loop that looks up ReBAC grants through folders (file → folder → upward)?
questions.hint: What happens at every step?

options.text: In a deep hierarchy or a list, every step runs a query, which can lead to N+1
options.why: Cut the queries by fetching the ancestor ids in one go or by using a materialized path.

options.text: None; a loop is always fast
options.why: A database call at every step makes big lists slow.

options.text: Dropping the loop and keeping a separate grant on every file is the only way
options.why: That makes new files and permission changes expensive to maintain. Inheritance is the advantage.

questions.q: A new developer forgot the tenant condition in the `exportAll()` query. Which measure makes this mistake nearly impossible?
questions.hint: Human memory, or an automatic mechanism?

options.text: A rule that says everyone must pay attention in code review
options.why: The mistake is something missing, which is hard to catch in review. Human attention is not a reliable barrier.

options.text: A Doctrine SQL filter that adds the tenant condition to every DQL query
options.why: Developers don't have to write the condition, so there is nothing to forget.

options.text: A separate repository class for each tenant
options.why: It doesn't reduce the room for error; they could forget the condition in a new query again.

options.text: Hiding other tenants' rows in Vue
options.why: By then the data has already reached the browser.

questions.q: Which level separates one tenant from another most strongly, and costs the most?
questions.hint: Not the next-door apartment, a separate house.

options.text: Row-level
options.why: The cheapest, but the riskiest.

options.text: Schema-per-tenant
options.why: In the middle: separate like an apartment, yet still one building (one database).

options.text: Database-per-tenant
options.why: Even a wrong query can't touch another tenant's data, but managing thousands of databases is expensive.

questions.q: What is the problem with the filter below?
questions.hint: Where does the tenant come from, and how does it get into the SQL?

options.text: The tenant comes from the client and goes straight into the SQL: both a data leak and SQL injection
options.why: Change `?tenant=` and you get someone else's data, and breaking out of the quotes gives SQL injection. You should use `$this->getParameter()` and the logged-in user's tenant.

options.text: No problem, since the filter is written
options.why: Even with a filter, the value inside it can't be trusted.

options.text: Only `sprintf` is slow
options.why: Speed isn't the issue; security is the real problem.

questions.q: In which of these places does the Doctrine tenant filter not protect you automatically?
questions.hint: Where there is no ORM/DQL, or no request-based login.

options.text: A report query written in raw DBAL SQL
options.why: The filter only attaches to ORM queries; it never sees raw SQL.

options.text: A handler running in a Messenger worker
options.why: With no request, the filter was never enabled, unless the handler enables it.

options.text: A plain ORM query using `findBy([...])` in a controller
options.why: This is an ORM query, and the filter applies to it when it is enabled.

options.text: An ORM query using `createQueryBuilder` in a controller
options.why: This is an ORM/DQL query, so the filter adds its condition automatically when it is enabled.

questions.q: The filter is enabled, but the `Employee` entity is saved without a tenant. What happens next?
questions.hint: What does `tenant_id = 7` do with a NULL?

options.text: The row matches no tenant's filter, so nobody can see it
options.why: NULL is never equal to 7. Stamp the tenant in a prePersist listener and make the column NOT NULL.

options.text: The row is visible to every tenant
options.why: That would be a leak, but the filter compares tenant_id to a number, and NULL matches none.

options.text: Doctrine sets the tenant by itself
options.why: The filter only affects reads. Nothing writes the tenant unless you do it.

questions.q: Two companies each have an employee with the email `a@x.com`, but a unique index on `user.email` stops the second one from registering. What is the fix?
questions.hint: Unique within what boundary?

options.text: Drop the unique index
options.why: Email must be unique within a tenant; dropping the index entirely would allow duplicate accounts.

options.text: A composite unique index on `(tenant_id, email)`
options.why: Uniqueness holds within a tenant; the same email is fine in different tenants.

options.text: Append a random number to the email
options.why: Changing the user's real email is the wrong path.

questions.q: One big customer sends hundreds of thousands of requests an hour and slows the other tenants. Which measures help?
questions.hint: Ways to limit resources per tenant.

options.text: A per-tenant limit in Symfony RateLimiter, with the tenant id as the key
options.why: Each tenant has its own bucket, so one tenant's rush doesn't squeeze the others.

options.text: A `statement_timeout` on heavy queries, and a separate queue/worker
options.why: It limits how much of the database and background capacity one tenant can occupy.

options.text: Keeping all tenants' limits in one shared bucket
options.why: Then one customer can empty the whole bucket and block the others.

options.text: Asking the customer to send fewer requests and changing nothing in code
options.why: You can't leave the system's stability to a customer's good manners.

questions.q: How is the code below weak?
questions.hint: What goes into the token, and what is kept in the database?

options.text: The token is guessable (user id + time), stored in plain form, and has no expiry or used flag
options.why: An attacker can guess the id and time to build the token; it is usable the moment the database leaks; and it works forever.

options.text: Only sha1 is old; sha256 would be safe
options.why: The kind of hash isn't the main problem. The input itself is guessable, so any hash can be guessed.

options.text: No problem, since the link goes by email
options.why: Sending by email is not security; the attacker can build the token himself without any inbox.

questions.q: Which behavior of a forgot-password endpoint opens a user enumeration gap?
questions.hint: How can an outsider tell whether an email exists?

options.text: 404 "user not found" when the email doesn't exist, 200 when it does
options.why: Seeing this difference, an attacker tests many emails and gets a list of users.

options.text: Always 202 with the same message
options.why: This is the correct behavior, not a gap.

options.text: Keeping a rate limit by IP
options.why: This slows enumeration down; it doesn't open a gap.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a correct reset implementation?
questions.hint: Think of a complete, single-use flow.

options.text: Storing the token in the database only as a SHA-256 hash
options.why: Even after a leak, the real token can't be recovered.

options.text: Revoking the user's refresh tokens after a successful reset
options.why: Otherwise a thief stays in with an old token.

options.text: A token lifetime of 30 days so the user can do it later
options.why: A long lifetime widens the window for attack; 15 to 60 minutes is enough.

options.text: Emailing the new password after the reset
options.why: A plain password sits in the inbox; send only a single-use link.

questions.q: The reset link's URL is built with `$request->getSchemeAndHttpHost()`. What can happen if an attacker sends `Host: evil.example`?
questions.hint: Which site will the link point to?

options.text: Nothing, since the email goes out from our server
options.why: The email does go out from us, but the link's host has been set by the attacker.

options.text: The link in the victim's email points to evil.example, and a click puts the token in the attacker's hands
options.why: This is Host header poisoning. The host should come from configuration.

options.text: Symfony changes the Host itself
options.why: To stop untrusted hosts you have to configure trusted_hosts and default_uri; it doesn't happen on its own.

questions.q: After resetting the password, the user clicked the link again. What should happen?
questions.hint: What does single-use mean?

options.text: Show the reset form again
options.why: If the same link kept working, a thief who reads the email could change the password all over again.

options.text: A message saying "the link is invalid or has expired"
options.why: A used token is marked used and won't work again. Keep the message generic.

options.text: Log them in directly
options.why: The link would become a way in without a password.

questions.q: Two tabs submit the same reset link at the same instant. Which code lets both succeed?
questions.hint: What happens between the isUsed() check and the flush()?

options.text: This one: both requests read the row as unused before either one writes
options.why: The check and the write are separate steps. Use one UPDATE ... WHERE used_at IS NULL and check that one row changed.

options.text: None: isUsed() always stops the second request
options.why: It only stops a request that arrives after the first has been saved. Simultaneous ones both see "unused".

options.text: None: hashing the token prevents it
options.why: Hashing protects a leaked database; it does nothing about two requests racing.

questions.q: Which measures keep the recovery path as strong as login?
questions.hint: The back door must not be weaker than the front door.

options.text: When MFA is lost, recovery codes issued in advance, otherwise a 24 to 72 hour wait and an email to every address
options.why: It makes fast deception hard and gives the real owner time to notice.

options.text: A rate limit by IP and email on the recovery endpoint
options.why: It stops brute force and enumeration.

options.text: Keeping security questions (mother's name, favorite city)
options.why: These answers can be guessed from social media; they are weak.

options.text: Support disabling MFA after hearing "it's me" on the phone
options.why: A simple path for social engineering.

questions.q: The .env below was committed. What is the most urgent step?
questions.hint: Once you assume it has leaked, first shut the path to the damage.

options.text: Delete the lines in the next commit
options.why: The values stay in the old commit, and anyone who cloned already has them.

options.text: Rotate the DB password and the Stripe key, and revoke the old ones
options.why: Revoking a leaked secret is what makes it useless. Everything else comes after.

options.text: Make the repository private
options.why: People who already copied it have the values, and a bot may have grabbed them earlier.

options.text: Change only APP_ENV to dev
options.why: APP_ENV is not a secret; changing it does nothing about the leaked keys.

questions.q: With the Symfony vault, which of these are safe to commit to git?
questions.hint: Which ones can't be used to read a secret on their own?

options.text: The encrypted secret files (config/secrets/prod/*)
options.why: They are encrypted with the public key and can't be read without the private key.

options.text: The public key (prod.encrypt.public.php)
options.why: A public key can only encrypt, not decrypt. Leaking it does no harm.

options.text: The private key (prod.decrypt.private.php)
options.why: Whoever gets this file can decrypt every secret, so it stays out of git.

options.text: A .env.local containing the production values
options.why: .env.local holds real values, which is exactly why it is git-ignored. Committing it would leak them directly.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below?
questions.hint: Who can read the code?

options.text: The secret is written in the code, so anyone with the repository gets the live key
options.why: The secret should come from the environment or the vault, via #[Autowire(env: ...)].

options.text: It should use a property instead of a const
options.why: Const or property, a value written in code ends up in git either way.

options.text: Sending a Bearer token in a header is wrong
options.why: A header is the right place. It is putting it in the URL that leaks it into logs.

questions.q: You must rotate a DB password with no downtime. What is the right order?
questions.hint: During the deploy, some servers will still be using the old password.

options.text: Change the existing password, then deploy the app
options.why: Between the password change and the end of the deploy, the app can't log in to the DB.

options.text: Create a new DB user, move the app to it, then disable the old user
options.why: At least one valid credential exists the whole time, so no request is blocked.

options.text: Shut everything down at 3 a.m. and change it
options.why: Even at night, that is downtime. If you can avoid it, you should.

options.text: Disable the old user first, then create the new one
options.why: In between there is no credential at all, and the app is down.

questions.q: Which of these follow the least privilege principle?
questions.hint: Think about the most damage one leaked key could do.

options.text: Giving the app's DB user only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on the tables it needs
options.why: Even with SQL injection, it can't DROP anything or touch other databases.

options.text: A separate API key for every service
options.why: If one leaks, only that service is hurt; the others stay separate.

options.text: One admin key shared by all services, so it is easy to remember
options.why: It is convenient, but one leak takes everything. That is the opposite of least privilege.

options.text: Giving developers live keys on their laptops, so debugging is easier
options.why: A stolen laptop or some malware would hand over the production keys directly.

questions.q: At 2 a.m. an alert shows 40 unknown servers started with your cloud access key. What is the first move?
questions.hint: Is the key still being used while you decide?

options.text: Create a new key, deploy it everywhere, and revoke the old one tomorrow
options.why: That is the no-downtime order, but here the attacker keeps spending for every hour the old key stays valid.

options.text: Revoke the key immediately, then create a new one and deploy it
options.why: The key is being abused right now, so cutting it off beats avoiding a few minutes of downtime.

options.text: Delete the commit that contained the key
options.why: The key has already been copied; deleting history does not stop anyone using it.

options.text: Wait until morning, when the team is online
options.why: The bill grows every minute, and the attacker may be reading data too.

questions.q: Ethan is building a purchase API. The request looks like { "product_id": 5, "price": 100 } and the server uses that price as given. Which STRIDE threat is this?
questions.hint: What if the customer sends the price as 50, or as 1?

options.text: Spoofing
options.why: Nobody got in under someone else's identity. The problem is trusting data the client sent.

options.text: Tampering: the server should take the price from the database, not from the client
options.why: Values sent by the client can be altered. Things like prices are always computed on the server.

options.text: Repudiation
options.why: That is about denying an action. Here the problem is that data can be altered.

options.text: Denial of service
options.why: Nothing here is about taking the service down; the damage is selling at the wrong price.

questions.q: Which STRIDE threat is the most obvious in the code below?
questions.hint: Could a user call this with someone else's invoice id?

options.text: Information disclosure: with no ownership check, other people's invoices can be seen
options.why: Any logged-in user can change the id and read someone else's invoice. It needs an object-level check (a voter).

options.text: Repudiation
options.why: This is a read endpoint; denying an action is not the main question here.

options.text: Spoofing, because the method is GET
options.why: Using GET is not what causes spoofing. The identity is fine here; the permission was never checked.

questions.q: Which of these data flows cross a trust boundary?
questions.hint: Think about where the level of trust changes.

options.text: A POST request from the browser to the Symfony API
options.why: The browser is outside our control, so this is the first boundary.

options.text: A webhook sent by the payment gateway
options.why: It is data sent by an outside company, so a fake webhook can get in if you don't verify the signature.

options.text: A call from one method of a controller to another
options.why: It is a call inside the same code; the zone of trust hasn't changed.

options.text: The validated API writing to your own database
options.why: It is an internal path. You still need parameterized queries, but this is not a trust boundary.

questions.q: Sarah is threat-modeling the refund feature and is short on time. Which arrow should she start with?
questions.hint: Where is the damage greatest?

options.text: Where money moves: customer to refund API, and API to gateway
options.why: Paths carrying money and personal data carry the most risk. Starting there catches the big holes even if time runs out.

options.text: Whichever is easiest to draw
options.why: Easy doesn't mean important. Order the work by level of risk.

options.text: The arrow few people know about
options.why: Unknown doesn't mean dangerous; the size of the damage and the likelihood are the yardstick.

options.text: No order, everything at once
options.why: You can't cover everything in half an hour, and with no order the biggest risk may be the one left out.

questions.q: A threat model shows that blocking one threat would take 3 weeks, but the damage is minor and the likelihood low. What is the best decision?
questions.hint: Compare the cost of the countermeasure with the damage.

options.text: Accept the risk and write down the reason
options.why: When the cost exceeds the damage, accepting is reasonable, as long as you record the decision and the reason.

options.text: Quietly delete the threat from the list
options.why: If you delete it, nobody will know later that it was considered.

options.text: Build the countermeasure no matter how long it takes
options.why: Not all threats are equal; other important work could be held up.

options.text: Cancel the whole feature
options.why: Canceling a whole feature over minor damage is out of proportion.

questions.q: What is the problem with the endpoint below?
questions.hint: What type could quantity be, and what value could it have? Is sku even there?

options.text: There is no validation: quantity could be negative, a string or missing
options.why: With #[MapRequestPayload] and a DTO using a type and Range, these are stopped right at the server boundary.

options.text: json_decode is slow; it should use simplexml
options.why: Speed is not the problem here; the problem is unvalidated values.

options.text: It should be GET, not POST
options.why: POST is right for creating an order. The HTTP method is not the security problem here.

options.text: Everything is fine, because the Vue form has checks
options.why: A request sent directly with curl never even touches Vue's checks.

questions.q: How would you fix the code below?
questions.code:
$sql = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = {$userId} AND status = '{$status}'";
$rows = $connection->executeQuery($sql)->fetchAllAssociative();
questions.hint: The values and the SQL need to travel on separate paths.

options.text: Escape $status with addslashes($status)
options.why: Escaping is brittle; some character-set tricks break it, and $userId doesn't even need a quote to be exploited.

options.text: Check with a regex that $status is only lowercase letters
options.why: It is good as an extra check, but it is not the main fix; the shape of the query stays the same.

options.text: Call executeQuery with two parameters: ... WHERE user_id = :uid AND status = :st
options.why: Both values travel to the database as parameters on a separate path, so they never become SQL instructions.

options.text: Give the database user read-only rights
options.why: It reduces the damage, but with injection all the data can still be read. It is an extra layer, not the main fix.

questions.q: Which of these in a comment area create an XSS risk?
questions.hint: Which ones put user-written text on the page without escaping?

options.text: <div v-html="comment.body"> in Vue
options.why: v-html runs the text as HTML; an would go right through.

options.text: {{ comment.body|raw }} in Twig
options.why: |raw turns off auto-escaping; on user-written text it is dangerous.

options.text: {{ comment.body }} in Vue
options.why: It is escaped by default; a script tag shows up as text and doesn't run.

options.text: Cleaning it with HtmlSanitizer, then displaying it
options.why: This is the remedy: only safe tags stay, and script or event handlers are dropped.

questions.q: Kevin posts the comment `Nice`. Ryan wants to keep the bold. Which fix is right?
questions.hint: Which fix removes the dangerous part and keeps the harmless part?

options.text: Sanitize the HTML (HtmlSanitizer on the server, or DOMPurify) and show the cleaned result
options.why: The bold tag stays, and the onerror attribute is cut, so nothing runs.

options.text: Delete the word "script" from every comment
options.why: The attack above has no "script" word at all; a blocklist always misses some form.

options.text: Keep v-html and add only a Content-Security-Policy header
options.why: CSP is a good second wall, but alone it leaves the hole open and only limits the damage.

options.text: Switch to {{ comment.body }}
options.why: It is safe, but the bold tag would then show up as literal text, so the feature is lost.

questions.q: Brian's app has an "import a photo from a URL" feature. Which measure best prevents SSRF?
questions.hint: Who should decide the list of places the server may go?

options.text: Checking whether the URL contains the word "localhost"
options.why: A blocklist is easy to dodge: 127.1, [::1], or a DNS name that points to 127.0.0.1.

options.text: A host allowlist, blocking private IPs (NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient), and turning off redirects
options.why: It stops the attack in three layers: the approved host, the resolved IP, and the redirect trick.

options.text: Rejecting every scheme except https
options.why: You can reach the internal network over https too; checking the scheme is only one part.

options.text: Keeping the response size small
options.why: A size limit helps against DoS, but even a small response can leak an access key.

questions.q: Which of these are safe alternatives or remedies for unserialize()?
questions.hint: Look for a path where no class's code starts on its own.

options.text: Take the data as JSON and read it into a DTO with #[MapRequestPayload]
options.why: JSON is only data; nothing outside the DTO's declared fields gets filled in, so no code runs.

options.text: unserialize($data, ['allowed_classes' => false])
options.why: No objects can be built, so no magic method runs. Still, JSON is better in new code.

options.text: Base64-encoding the serialized data and sending it in a cookie
options.why: Base64 is neither secrecy nor protection; an attacker can decode and encode it easily.

options.text: Keeping the name of the cart cookie secret
options.why: Hiding the name stops nothing; the cookie sits with the client.

questions.q: What is the safest way to store an uploaded file?
questions.hint: Who should control the file's name, location and type?

options.text: In public/uploads/ under the client's name, allowlisting by extension
options.why: The name and extension are in the client's hands; if shell.php can run in a public folder, the server is taken over.

options.text: Verify the type from the content, use your own UUID name, and store it outside the web root
options.why: The server controls the name, type and location; the file can't be reached directly by URL.

options.text: Accept the file based on the Content-Type the client sent
options.why: The client can set the Content-Type to anything.

questions.q: Adam's registration code is below. What is the problem?
questions.hint: If a thief gets the dump, how many guesses per second can they make?

options.text: SHA-256 is fast and unsalted, so the hashes are easy to crack; it needs UserPasswordHasherInterface
options.why: A fast hash makes every guess cheap. A slow, salted argon2id or bcrypt is what passwords need.

options.text: persist() and flush() can't be called together
options.why: Calling them together is normal; the problem is the kind of hash.

options.text: It should have been encrypted with AES, not hashed
options.why: Encryption is reversible; if the key is stolen, every password leaks at once.

options.text: md5 would be better than sha256 because it is shorter
options.why: MD5 is even faster and broken, so it is even worse.

questions.q: Which of these are correct rules for storing passwords?
questions.hint: Does a password ever need to be read back?

options.text: A slow, salted hash (argon2id or bcrypt)
options.why: Each guess is expensive, and the same password produces different hashes.

options.text: Keeping Symfony's password_hashers set to auto, so old hashes upgrade themselves
options.why: Even if the best algorithm changes in future, hashes get renewed at login.

options.text: Encrypting with AES, so "I forgot my password" can send the old one
options.why: A feature that sends the password back is itself a bad design. You send a reset link, not the old password.

options.text: Plain text in the database, but with a password on the database
options.why: Once someone gets past the database password, everything is open. Each user's password must be protected individually.

questions.q: An app has an encrypted database disk, yet SQL injection leaked users' SSNs. What was needed?
questions.hint: In front of whom does disk encryption stand open?

options.text: App-level encryption on the SSN field, with the key kept outside the database
options.why: Even if the database leaks, the SSN can't be read without the key.

options.text: A stronger algorithm for the disk encryption
options.why: Disk encryption stands open to a running database, so changing the algorithm doesn't help.

options.text: TLS on the DB connection
options.why: TLS stops eavesdropping on the way; the answer to a SQL injection comes back in the clear all the same.

options.text: Base64-encoding the SSN
options.why: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone can reverse it in one line.

questions.q: Why is the encryption in the code below not safe?
questions.hint: What happens if you use the same key and the same nonce twice?

options.text: The nonce is fixed, so it gets reused with the same key and the encryption breaks
options.why: Every time, take a new nonce from random_bytes() and store it with the ciphertext.

options.text: It shouldn't call base64_encode
options.why: Base64 is only for convenient storage; it isn't a problem.

options.text: MD5 would have been better than secretbox
options.why: MD5 is a hash, not encryption; you could never get the data back.

questions.q: What are the advantages of envelope encryption with a KMS?
questions.hint: Where does the master key live, and what does it take to change it?

options.text: The master key never leaves the KMS to reach the app or the database
options.why: Even if the app is hacked, no copy of the master key can be found.

options.text: Changing the master key only means locking the data keys again
options.why: The data doesn't have to be re-encrypted, so rotation is cheap.

options.text: One key for all the data, so it is simple
options.why: That is the opposite of an envelope; if one key leaks, all the data opens.

options.text: You can keep the master key in the app, without a KMS
options.why: Then you lose the benefit of a KMS. If the app holds the master key, it is also a way to steal it.

questions.q: Which steps does the app take to read a value stored with envelope encryption?
questions.hint: Which key goes to the KMS, and which key comes back?

options.text: Send the locked data key to the KMS and get the open data key back
options.why: Only the KMS can open the locked key, and only the small data key comes back.

options.text: Decrypt the data with the open data key, then wipe the key from memory
options.why: The open key is needed only for the moment of decryption. Keeping it around widens the window for theft.

options.text: Ask the KMS to decrypt the whole column of data directly
options.why: A KMS handles small keys, not bulk data. Direct KMS encryption is limited to a few kilobytes.

options.text: Fetch the master key from the KMS and decrypt locally
options.why: The master key never leaves the KMS; that is the whole point.

questions.q: The app's logs sometimes contain a whole request body, including passwords and SSNs. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Which step works even when someone makes a mistake?

options.text: Tell everyone: don't write passwords to the logs
options.why: People will make mistakes. What a machine can guarantee shouldn't be left to a rule.

options.text: Redact the sensitive keys as [REDACTED] with a Monolog processor, and stop logging bodies
options.why: It is written once and works on every log channel, and less information is written in the first place.

options.text: Give only admins access to the log files
options.why: A good extra layer, but logs travel to many tools and stay for a long time; it doesn't stop the leak.

options.text: Set the log level to error everywhere
options.why: Changing the level doesn't change which data goes in.

questions.q: The redactor masks keys named `password` and `token`. A developer writes `$logger->info("Login for $phone failed")`. What ends up in the log?
questions.hint: What exactly does the redactor look at?

options.text: The phone number in plain text, because the redactor only checks the names of context keys
options.why: The number is inside the message string, which the processor never inspects.

options.text: [REDACTED], because the redactor finds phone numbers by itself
options.why: It matches key names from a fixed list. It has no idea what a phone number looks like.

options.text: Nothing, because Monolog drops messages that contain personal data
options.why: Monolog writes whatever it is given. Keeping PII out is the developer's job.

questions.q: What is the biggest problem in the CI script below?
questions.hint: Is the code that was tested the same as the code that gets deployed?

options.text: `update` pulls the newest versions; the tested code can differ from the lock file's, and a poisoned version could come in
options.why: In CI use `composer install` followed by `composer audit`; keep `update` for a PR.

options.text: deploy should run before phpunit
options.why: Testing first is right; the problem is how versions are decided.

options.text: --no-interaction should be removed
options.why: No interaction is better in CI. The problem is elsewhere.

options.text: There is no problem; the newest version is the safest
options.why: New does not mean safe; supply chain attacks arrive in exactly the new versions.

questions.q: Which of these reduce supply chain risk?
questions.hint: Which ones pin versions or catch known vulnerabilities?

options.text: Committing composer.lock and running `composer install` in CI
options.why: Every build uses exactly the same, vetted versions.

options.text: Running `composer audit --locked` on every build
options.why: If a known vulnerable package is found the build breaks, so you find out at once.

options.text: Setting every package's version to "*" so you always get the newest
options.why: That lets any poisoned new version in by itself. It is the opposite of pinning versions.

options.text: Updating all packages together once a year
options.why: A giant update makes it hard to tell what broke, and vulnerabilities stay open for the whole year in between. Small steps are better.

questions.q: Dana's deploy pipeline keeps a long-lived AWS access key as a secret. Which is the best improvement?
questions.hint: If it is stolen, how long will the key keep working?

options.text: Use OIDC to get temporary credentials on each run, only on the main branch, through a role with narrow permissions
options.why: Even if stolen, it is useless within hours, and it can only do limited things.

options.text: Rename the secret to an obscure name
options.why: Hiding the name doesn't make the value any safer.

options.text: Hardcode the key in the code and keep it in a private repository
options.why: Even worse: everyone with the code, and all of the history, gets the key.

options.text: Run the deploy on every PR so it is always verified
options.why: A PR can edit the workflow or the code it runs, so unreviewed code would hold the secrets. Deploy only after a merge to a vetted branch.

questions.q: A stranger opens a PR from a fork against Nicole's repo. What can they do with this workflow?
questions.code:
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  test:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: composer install && vendor/bin/phpunit
        env:
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
questions.hint: Whose code does the job run, and who holds the key?

options.text: Nothing: GitHub never gives secrets to fork PRs
options.why: That holds for plain `pull_request`. `pull_request_target` runs with the secrets.

options.text: Add a composer script or a test that sends the key to their server
options.why: The job checks out the PR's code and runs it with the key in the environment.

options.text: Nothing: the code is only tested, never deployed
options.why: Testing means running the code. Running is all a thief needs.

options.text: Read only the public files of the repo
options.why: They can run code with your secret in its environment, which is far worse.

questions.q: Which framework applies in which situation?
questions.hint: Look at which data you touch.

options.text: GDPR, if you hold personal data of customers in Europe
options.why: Wherever the company is, touching EU residents' data brings GDPR.

options.text: PCI DSS, if you touch or process card data
options.why: A system that touches cards is under PCI. If you don't touch them, the scope is small.

options.text: A SOC 2 report, if B2B customers ask for proof of your security
options.why: Large corporate customers usually want to see a SOC 2 audit report.

options.text: HIPAA, certainly, for a school attendance app
options.why: HIPAA is for US health information; it doesn't apply to an attendance app.

questions.q: Under GDPR a user asks to be deleted, but the money records of their purchases must legally be kept for 5 years. What do you do?
questions.hint: Can the money records be separated from the person's identity?

options.text: Delete the user row and all their orders
options.why: Legal records can't be deleted, and the foreign keys would break too.

options.text: Refuse the request, because the records have to be kept
options.why: Identifying data can be deleted; refusing the whole request is wrong.

options.text: Anonymize the name, email and phone; keep the money records; write the event to the audit log
options.why: The person can't be identified, yet the legal duty is met and the data relationships stay intact.

options.text: Just set a "deleted" flag and keep the real data
options.why: That isn't deletion; if the data leaks, everything can still be read.
